We've owned a whole set of these for our dogs and cats; they've never broken, warped, or discolored in all the years we've had them. One star off because loading the battery into it is not unlike breaking into Fort Knox if Fort Knox were guarded by flying nanosharks. I originally bought nupro as a supplement for a foster dog who had mange.  I chose to cook her meals at home and I wanted to supplement her with something to help ensure she was getting everything she needed.  Two years at the shelter, suffering from severe demodectic mange leading to major hairloss, and within three weeks of a new diet, she had most of her hair back and was adopted.  After the success I saw with her, I bought it for our shar pei.  Our shar pei suffers from flea allergies and many other typical pei ailments (thin coat, skin issues, yeast infections, ear infections, etc).  It was important to me that it be grain free as we suspect she may have an underlying grain allergy. Nupro fit the bill. This stuff worked WONDERS.  Now at 14 months, she has a thick, shiny coat.  Our vet was impressed by the improvement in her coat quality, from bald to beautiful.  I use it on all of my fosters who are a little under the weather and need a boost.  It continues to be a part of my shar pei's daily regiment and will continue to do so for the rest of her life. I cannot say enough good things.  I recommend this to those who want a full, healthy coat among the many other benefits it has to offer.

I came across this product while researching kelp to decrease plaque and tartar on my Sheltie.  2 months later, my sister's  3 dogs (ahem, children)  and my mom's pooch are on this supplement.  I guess the most astonishing thing we've seen is this:  Georgia is a 15 year old cocker mix who had become pitiful looking.  First of all, she was covered in these wart like things---literally covered.  The vet would express some of them, but nothing took them away.  She is my sisters dog and I would not even touch her because the warts grossed me out.  Secondly, she had lost so much oh her hair that we called her baboon butt and her tail looked like the Grinches Christmas tree.  Seriously, you could hold it up and it had a few scraggly hairs hanging off a bald tail.  Thirdly, she was very gray.  So, I had not seen Georgia in about a month and when she walked in I thought my sister had a new dog.  Georgia's is now a luscious, glossy black ( except for her face) her fur is thick, soft and her tail  fur is completely full.  It truly is mind blowing and I would not have believed it had I not seen it.  Her warts are almost completely gone and she has so much energy.  I swear her eyesight and hearing are better but my sis does not agree with that.  As far as my 9 year old Lily- she acts like a 2 year old now.  My sisters other 2 dogs have the softest, silkiest fur you have ever seen and are the picture of health.  Just started my moms buddy on this and sending some home with my brother for his Romeo.  If I could but stock in this company I would.  Oh-  in terms of Lily's plaque?  Gone, period.  And I could not even break it off with a scraper.  We actually make homemade dog food (chicken, kale, sweet potato, broccoli, etc. no grain) and I just mix this in as I process it, freeze and pull out daily.  We don't give the pets a scoop a day- a teaspoon for the little guys, a tablespoon for my 30 pounder.We are all joking that we humans are going to start taking this!

Our dogs love it.  We rescued two woofs and one of them was severely abused.  Mange, fungal infection, abuse, no fur...horrible skin.  Dr. told us that he probably wouldn't get his fur back.  The rescue folks suggested Nupro Gold as they've seen wonders with this product.  It's hard to say if his fur would have grown back on it's own (and some of it on his face did not return) without the supplement, but we did use it and his coat is now beautiful. good for my dogs joints and also lots of vitamins,  makes my dogs coats soft and seems to keep them healthy , been buying this for a while now

This is absolutely not an alternative to or replacement for a refractometer. But if you're in a pinch and need to not spend the extra few bucks for a refractometer, you can probably get by with this. Just please understand what you're getting and the potential downfalls of relying solely on a hydrometer.

I've been using hydrometers for over 35 years.  This one would give me three different readings in three different attempts to check specific gravity in my aquarium.  Screwed up my salt levels in the tank by trusting this.  Corals are very unhappy.

After reading the instructions, keeping it rinse with regular water after use and discarding the first test each time I use it my readings still will not go past 1.016! This is even after adding more salt to the aquarium to bring it up to the 1.025 I need. Now I have no way of know what my salinity is until I purchase a refractometer for more accurate results which also puts a delay on me adding any inhabitants to the tank.I even gave it a second chance, I actually purchased saltwater from my local fish store which is pre-mixed at a salinity of 1.025. When I did a test on it...still got 1.016. Needless to say I will be throwing this item away.

There are mixed feelings about using a hydrometer to measure specific gravity of the water. but there are some ways to keep on getting accurate readings. one is , pour water in slowly, make sure all the fresh water is out so measure the first time and then dump it and measure again. Normally that gives the more accurate reading.  and always make sure there is no bubbles on the measuring unit. bubbles can greatly affect the reading.  Definitely a lot cheaper than a refractometer. I will get one later but for now this will do, since im just starting.

I happen to live near the ocean,, so I have the luxury of testing it against a control system.  I took several samples of ocean water at various depths and away from shore to see what the actualy salinity was.  Then I made a mark on it to set the salinity of my fish tank.. (.038) anyway,,  I live in the south pacific in the marshall islands.. First off, my dog (85 lb German Shepherd) has pannus. The purpose of doggles is to protect his eyes from UV light so that he doesn't go blind. I could care less about the coolness factor, this review is strictly based on the ability to protect my dogs eyes from the sun, and his comfort in wearing them.Second, I'm writing the same review for all the doggles, as a comparison, so you don't have to go looking through my other reviews to see how well the other types of doggles worked, or didn't work.Third, I only make my dog wear them when it is sunny or overcast outside. I generally try to take him for walks/runs when it is either early morning/evening, or cloudy days. But he's full of energy, so I have to take him out on sunny days. This is when he wears doggles.With the disclaimers aside:1st choice:  Doggles Mesh EyewearI only recently tried these, and wish I had tried them sooner. I think what kept me from buying these is that in the photos, it appears as if your dog is not able to see through these, and because it only protects from 50 to to 60% of UV light. After spending ridiculous amounts of money in search for the perfect eye protection on every kind of doggle out there, this has become my first choice, though still far from perfect.My dog can see very well with these, tolerates these the best out of all the other doggles. Will play with these on, and even chase a ball if other dogs are around chasing the same ball. I have noticed that sometimes he can't follow the toy as well, but that seems to be based on how fast the toy is flying and how high I throw it. So I still have to change how I play with him, but at least now he will play with eye protection on, which is huge.The mesh is very light, which is why I think he doesn't mind it. It is kind of awkward looking as the mesh has pointy ends that cause it to stick out and not be laying directly on his eyes. I had my dog wear these for a full day once, and when coming back inside, I noticed he didn't rub his eyes against the couch as much as he does with other doggles.The only reason I can't give this five stars is because it is only 50 to 60% uv protection rather than a 100% as offered with other doggles. This is a concern for me as the UV rays can really damage my dogs eyes due to the pannus. However, since my dog doesn't try to take these off anywhere near as much as the other doggles, I feel he gets a lot more protection from these since he actually keeps them on.Since trying these, I have bumped down the ranking on the other doggles as noted below.1st and 2nd choice: Doggles Large K9 Optix sunglasses, framelessThese are by no means perfect, and I fear the day they get broken. So far they have lasted several months with taking extreme good care of them. The reason they are one of my top choices is because they are 100% UV protection and my dog minds them the least (with the exception of the mesh doggles which are half the UV protection). I think what he hates about most doggles is that they have a bulky and heavy frame (from a dog's perspective), and they are not one lens, thus making them heavier on his head, and reducing his visibility. With these frameless doggles he does generally well, and is only intolerant of them when he's bored. He doesn't try to take these off as much, and as long as I have him distracted (going to a new place or chasing a critter), he doesn't mind them. He will more often than not play ball or catch a Frisbee with these on, but sometimes not. I wish I could give these five stars, but they are flimsy, and will fall apart eventually. I gave it four stars simply because they have held together thus far, with extra care. What really made this my top choice, is that they are frameless. I can see a huge difference in how my dog sees through these doggles in comparison to other doggles. So this gets first place simply for his comfort in vision. The straps fit nicely behind his ears and under his chin. If only they were made a little more sturdy...I am making these both my first and second choice because the mesh eyewear only offers half of the UV protection that these do, and I can't use the mesh eyewear on really bright sunny days due to lack of the UV protection.2nd choice: Doggles OriginalZThe doggles originalZ only come with one color lens, which really isn't a big deal, but I have learned that even on overcast days, my dog needs eye protection, and he's less tolerant of these on overcast days versus on very sunny days. I think the darkness of the lens may reduce his visibility. He tries to paw his doggles off more so than with the frameless pair, but he minds these less than the ILS doggles. Overall, I'm happy with these because he does do fairly well with them when distracted, but I can tell he dislikes them. He usually will not chase a ball or Frisbee with these on, especially if there are other dogs around. I think he can't see the ball/Frisbee as well, and other dogs can, so he just gives up. Unless we're doing something new and exciting, he generally will find a shady spot, lay down, and watch the world play around him. It's sad to see him this way, but going blind will be worse for him, so I keep making him wear them. The doggles are well designed with the strap that goes behind his head and under his chin, which is easily adjustable, and vent holes on the sides of the doggles so that his eyes don't sweat/fog up.3rd choice: Doggles ILSI started out with the ILS doggles since they were the newest doggle out, and I liked the idea of the interchangeable lenses. I tried several colors of lenses, and found that my dog minds the brown lenses the least. It is nice to be able to remove the lenses that are scratched up and replace them with shiny new ones, and it's also nice to put in the clear lenses for overcast days when I want my dog to be able to see more, with the darkest lenses on really sunny days. So why not my favorite doggle? The dog hates them. The design is almost the same as the originalZ, with a few differences. The straps seem about the same as the originalZ, and the vent holes only differ in shape. The nose piece seems to be further apart than the originalZ, and even though the frame, when compared to the originalZ when not on, seems the same, they are a lot bulkier when on. I also found the foam that is between the doggles and the dogs eye is a little different, and seems to fall apart easier than the originalZ. The doggles company actually was kind enough to throw in some free foam with my latest order, but even super gluing it didn't seem to hold it well in place. Because the ILS doggles are much bulkier than the originalZ, and the dog hates bulky things on his face, he tries harder with these than any other doggles to get them off. Often, I find him running back to me with his doggles all distorted on his face with the straps all tangled. I have no idea how he manages, but it's sad to see him running back to me for help to fix his doggles, which I'm sure he's hoping I take off. No way would he even consider chasing a ball or catching a Frisbee with these on.Last choice: Doggles K9 Optix Blue Rubber Gradient Frame with Smoke Lens SunglassesThese are almost frameless, top of the frame is very thin, so my dog didn't seem to mind them as much, however, they broke within a week, even with very careful use, and constant watching of my dog so that he doesn't paw at them, and taking care to put them in a safe place when not in use. These were my favorite except for the fragility of them, until I found the frameless.Okay, for those designers out there that want to make the perfect doggle, I hope you are reading this. You need a single lens doggle that is still very durable, sturdily built, and not too bulky. Basically, a single lens across both eyes, with a very light frame if any, such as the mesh with a softer plastic that is still 100% UV protection. Dogs are not human and do not see like humans, so why only create something that works for humans is beyond me. The frames in between the eyes are bothersome to the dog, and the bulk of most doggles (especially the ILS) causes discomfort. I actually bought a pair of ski goggles for humans and ended up sewing a chin strap to it to see if that would work, but it was too bulky and he was able to get them shook off by just shaking his head. But I could tell that his eyesight was just fine with the single lens.Lastly, when back inside and we remove the doggles, my dog immediately runs to the couch and rubs his eyes against it, which we talked to the dog eye specialist about. It was suggested, that after wearing doggles, rather than let the dog rub his eyes against objects, that we put icepacks on his eye area. Just a little hint for those who have the same problem.

So, I've always been against  invisible fences  for dogs because I don't like the idea of some mystery beeping and zapping that they can't see coming, and I don't 100% trust them to keep a determined dog in his space.  Then I got the opportunity to analyze how this model worked out for a neighbor.  And then I had no choice but to try it with my own rescue baby.  Here are their stories...The neighbors have a male boxer, and they began training him on this system as a young puppy.  They keep him outside at all times (which I hate!!), but for the most part, the system seems to work to keep him safe in his yard.  He's also right between 2 very busy roads (which makes me extra nervous), but he manages to stay in bounds 95% of the time.  The times he has left bounds were when he was desperate and his battery had stopped working. Most times he doesn't even go close to the actual bounds, so he never hears the beeping, but this one day, his owner was next door, and the dog really really wanted to be with him.  He went for it, and he never got beeped or zapped because the battery died.  NOTE:  THE BATTERIES DIE QUICKLY WHEN THEY'RE ALWAYS ON, SO CHECK THEM FREQUENTLY!!!!!  The other times he has left his bounds, suffering the zapping, were on holidays with fireworks (4th of July, New Year's Eve).  Seriously, if you have a dog, keep an eye on it during fireworks, or keep them very safe inside.  They'll be scared inside, too, but at least they'll be safe.  One of the worst problems with this poor dog being on this system 24/7 is that he has a huge furless lump on his neck where the metal things jab him.  For the record, the warnings/instructions say not to leave the unit on your dog for longer than 12 hours at a time, so I fault the owners for leaving it on him all the time.  Also, surprisingly, the metal things don't seem to bother the dogs (at least not boxers), even if they look uncomfortable to me.  This boxer doesn't even seem to mind his huge lump, but I'm very disturbed by it.All that said....  I then rescued a boxer, about a year or two old when I got her.  She had been living in a foster home with a fenced yard, so she was used to having freedom to run around with fenced boundaries.  Unfortunately, my home doesn't have a fence nor any way to fence it in.  I stressed so much about how to give my dog freedom to run around, but still keep her safe within the boundaries of our yard.  Plus, training a year old dog can be tough.  A wireless fence was the only option I could come up with.  She's very much an indoor dog, but she goes outside to use the bathroom and play.  Training her on this system was a little difficult at first. It took her a while to get comfortable with the yard again, and she would relapse to the porch if she heard beeping.  That's kind of good that she would come back and stay close to the house, but it defeats the purpose if she isn't running around getting exercise in the yard.  After some more time, we actually stopped using the collar on her (which she never associated with the beeping or zapping), and she eventually got used to the yard.  The good news, and I'll credit this system, is that she did learn to stay in the bounds of the yard.  No specific bounds, and she actually doesn't go as far around the yard as she can.  But basically, it did what I needed it to do.  Even though I don't use the system anymore, I feel like $200 was a worthwhile investment just to train her to hang out in the yard. This is a classic power filter that has been around for a long time.  Many competing brands of power filters have come and gone over the many years that this filter has been in production.  And this one continues to sell today.  This design has a lot going for it.  It is inexpensive to purchase, reliable, easy to set up, easy to clean, and the replacement media are affordable.This filter is what is known as a HOB (hangs on the back of the aquarium) power filter.  The hang-on-the-back power filter design usually cater to the casual aquarist.  That is not to say that advanced aquarists do not use them.  It is just that there are other filter designs that do a better job of mechanical, chemical, and biological filtration than the simple power filter.  The main advantage to the power filter is the ease of set up.  There are no hoses to cut, and holes do not need to be drilled into the fish tank.  A small motor-driven impeller pulls water from the tank, passes it through the filter media, and then releases the water back into the tank.  All this is done by sending the water over the top edge of the tank.I can recommend this Aquaclear to someone with a freshwater tank of less than 20 gallon capacity.  It runs reliably and quietly.  If you hear a lot of noise coming from the filter, please remove the energizer (motor) and check the impeller.  Also, make sure that the inlet tube is fully inserted on top of the impeller well.  The mechanical filter is basically a coarse sponge.  You can rinse this sponge out to remove excess debris and put it back in the filter.  Just be sure to rinse it out using dechlorinated water, or waste water from the tank itself.  Unless this sponge becomes hopelessly clogged with debris (possible if you have live plants), you will not need to replace it.  The ceramic rings that are included were designed to provide a place for beneficial bacteria to colonize and attach to.  The carbon pack will need to be replaced.  How often will depend on your tank's particular situation.A canister filter will usually provide superior mechanical and chemical filtration capabilities in comparison.  However, depending on the design, maintenance will usually consume more of your time.  Wet/Dry filtration provides superior bio filtration, but will usually be more expensive.  The Penguin (Marineland) power filter brand, with their bio-wheel, is said to be better at biological filtration than this and most other competing power filter design.  It is priced competitively with the Aquaclear.  However, with the Penguin, you will have to regularly buy their filter media.  The Aquaclear gives you more flexibility and more room in the filter box.  I have used an Emperor 400 in the past on a large cichlid tank.  The Emperor, which is similar in design to the Penguins, was made by Marineland.  Very good design, but again, you will have to purchase their filter media on a regular basis.  With the Aquaclear, you can buy your own filter bag, buy carbon in bulk, and save money over the life of the filter.Why 4 stars instead of 5?  The design allows for a lot of water by-pass.  Power filters allow for some by-pass to compensate for clogged filter pads.  The Aquaclears seem to allow more by-pass than its competitors.  Also, because of the coarse design of the mechanical filter sponge, a lot of the smaller particles pass through.  The prepackaged carbon bag fits snugly in the filter box of this filter, perhaps packing the carbon granules tighter than they need to be.  The water simply just flows around the bag and only makes contact with the carbon on the edges of the bag.  I have also found that the carbon media is not very good at removing tannins from mopani wood from the water.This is a very inexpensive filter to maintain.  I know a fellow hobbyist who does not use carbon.  He just rinses the sponge during his water changes, puts it back in, and turns the filter back on.  His only expense with this filter was the initial purchase price.  I use carbon, so there is a little bit of regular expense for me.  But there are those who choose not to use carbon.  Some cichlid keepers blame carbon as a possible cause of Hole-in-the-Head disease.  I am not an expert and clearly the issues of carbon's relationship to this disease is beyond my qualifications to discuss.  Since I no longer keep cichlids, I have continued to use carbon.

Pros -1) easy to maintain2) easy t0 use custom media like purigen, Poly media, for polishing water and carbon for removing medication3) does a good job of aerating the waterCons1) it is clear so not so good for bio filtering, (light dramatically reduces the ability of nitrification bacteria)2) Flow rate is dramatically reduced if the water is lower then a couple of inches, so not useful in an amphibian tank.3) aerates the water which is not desirable if using CO2 injection or even on a low tech planted tank4) current flow is poor on the 1/2 of tank opposite the filter (a problem with all waterfall filters). The problem with them is that they will release the ammonia they have absorbed if salt is added to the water. This is very bad as the first step after doing a water change when an ammonia spike occurs is to add salt to the water along with something like seachem prime, If you do not remove the zeolite before doing this then the problem will be compounded.I also do not use carbon on a regular bases. AquaClears are one of my favorite brands of hang on the back filters. They are fairly compact, well-made, affordable, and easy to set up, use, and clean.The media baskets in AC filters are quite large compared to many other filters, so you can cram quite a lot in there if you want to. The media is stacked in the tray vertically, so the coarse sponge should be on the bottom, with the biological media and fine filtration on top of that. I also use a cut up sponge on the intake as a prefilter to protect the impeller from any sand that might get kicked up from the bottom. The sponges are inexpensive and can be reused for quite a long time if you clean them regularly.The flow rate of the water can be adjusted by rotating the intake tubing away from the impeller, which is good when you are feeding and want the food to stay at the surface. I usually allow the filter to run at maximum flow most of the time and use a baffle I made from an old soft drink bottle to keep from agitating the water too much. I would recommend getting one filter size up from the tank you plan on using it for though. I use the AC50 on a 20g tank, and I feel that it is an appropriate amount of filtration. Without the baffle it may have been too much agitation, however it works very well with my setup.Overall I would say that an AquaClear filter is a good investment for most tanks. This is what  I did to fix it, but listen to me and fix it before you lose it: I had to cut the collar off the nylon part and attach it to a new collar. I may be female but I don't sew. Superglue is my friend. I glued it to a leather collar. It's held this way for months, even getting wet in the pool.However! If you take the end of the collar that has no  stop  built in and fold it a bit, superglue it together, it will make it where the buckle can't just slide off. You have to hold it down to turn the collar off, but you have to watch it and make sure it blinks a certain number of times, indicating it's really turning off. When you turn it on, you have to make sure it blinks the right amount of green blinks (one= light shock, 2= medium shocks, 3=the  meanest  shocks). There is a time delay in the blinking. If  you have a dog that goes in and out a million times a day like mine, you will be putting it on and taking it off all day long. (NOTE, the dog shouldn't wear the collar while inside, it can cause skin irritation because it's so tight by necessity and it jabs into their trachea while eating, so please don't just leave it on your dog while he or she comes in, that's not nice!) I got fed up when I noticed that I had inadvertently changed it to test mode (blinks orange) or changed the shock setting, and I got tired of standing there, peering at the tiny little cell phone led sized lights waiting for the blinks, so we just leave it on 24/7. It's really much easier. The battery lasted at least 3 months even with it on all the time. Just order a 2 pack of extra batteries and keep them around. They're about $6 if I remember correctly. In a year's time we haven't used the one it came with and the spare- well worth the time saved by not having to decipher the blinking lights.Also, after this amount of time the white writing on the unit itself is wearing off. If I didn't know how to use it, I might not be able to figure it out because the writing is nearly gone.Some how to tips- make sure it's tight on the dog's neck. It works by vibration and this ensures that your dog doesn't get shocked from another dog's barking. Make it tight but obviously don't choke the dog. I keep it above, higher on the neck, more towards the chin on my dog, above his regular collar. He doesn't dislike wearing it. He stands still and happily lets me put it on him every day.A last word of advice- I rescue dogs and work in a animal rescue. Please have current name/phone # tags on your dog at all times, and spay and neuter your dog! Don't let your outdoor cat who has no collar and is not neutered or spayed roam free, or you may find your cat eaer tipped and altered by someone like me who traps them and takes them into be altered. Most acid loving fish will do fine in PH up to 8 if acclimatized.The 2 main causes of fish deaths is an ammonia spike and PH swings from having too low of a dkh.The dkh (carbonate hardness) is far more critical then PH. Most experienced fish keepers keep it at least 5. When dkh gets below 3 a dangerous condition is produced that will likely kill fish. Over time the dkh will fall in your aquarium due to the acids produced in your filter. Water changes or adding an appropriate buffer should be done when the KH falls below a target level.PH is controlled by 3 factors, KH, CO2 and the amount of acid produced in your filter.My tap water has a dkh of 8, I am setting up a tank for a Dwarf puffer. I found these fish do not acclimatize as well as most acid loving fish. This prompted me to experiment with the Neutral regulatorAfter adding a good amount over a period of 3 days I saw little change, I concluded that it is not really great at lowering PH.Next I started with a new batch of tap water and used Acid Buffer to lower my dkh to about 1. I then added some Neutral Regulator and tested my water the next day, The PH was about 7 and the dkh was 6.If your tap water has low dkh it is likely to be low in trace minerals, or If you use RO or distilled water it will lack trace minerals need for fish. In this case you can use an alkaline buffer (commercial or baking soda) or the neutral regulator to raise the KH. You will also need to add trace minerals which will raise the GH.It is important when doing a water change to not make drastic changes in your tank, A change of over .3 ph, more then 2dkh or a change temperature more then 2 degrees F can cause problems.In conclusion I found the best way for me to use this product was to add acid buffer to drop my dkh to around 1 then use the Neutral regulator to make the water stable.What you need to add to your water, if anything, depends on state of your tap water. I highly recommend that you include a KH test as part of your weekly maintenance.

Getting plants to grow and flourish in a typical home aquarium can be a challenge.Allow me to clarify.  Getting most of the popular and widely available aquatic plants to grow in a fish tank with sufficient lighting is not very hard.  What is a challenge is getting the plants to grow at a rate fast enough to be able to keep algae under control.  Under the care of an inexperienced aquarists, what starts out at as tank full of lush, green plants quickly turn into an algae farm.  Soon after, algae takes over.  The aquarists takes measures to fight the algae, and more often than not, loses the battle.Is it really necessary to add a substrate fertilizer to a planted tank?  Would it not be much easier to simply dose with a liquid fertilizer on a regular basis?  The answers to those questions would depend on the plants, and your specific situation.  All I can provide here are some advise, based on personal experience as well as information learned from other hobbyists.It is not entirely correct to assume that you cannot fertilize the roots without the use of a substrate fertilizer.  When you add liquid fertilizer to the water, eventually, that fertilizer will work its way down into the substrate.  Anything you put in the water will also make it down into the substrate.  In most cases, a substrate fertilizer like this Flourish Tabs is not necessary if you already add liquid fertilizer.  The principle also works in both directions.  When you add a solid fertilizer to the substrate, eventually it will dissolve and make its way to the water column.There are some specific situations in which using a solid, substrate fertilizer will have an advantage.  For my situation, I wanted to fertilize the plants growing on the substrate, but avoid fertilizing the floating plants.  That is not entirely possible, but with root tabs, you can deliver the ingredients to the plant roots before they make it up to the floating plants.  In other words, the ingredients will be at a higher concentration down in the substrate, while it is slowly diffusing into the water column.  Theoretically, you are encouraging the growth of the rooted plants more aggressively than you are encouraging the growth of the floating plants.  Theoretically, you are also keeping algae under control by avoiding dumping a high concentration of fertilizer in the water.  This is theoretical since we know that algae can do quite well with just a small amount of fertilizer.What is a clear advantage is that a solid, substrate fertilizer is low maintenance.  You can add these tablets to the substrate and not have to worry about adding liquid fertilizer on a frequent basis.  The solid tabs can last a long time and the effects continue even after it has dissolved.  The ingredients will slowly migrate upwards into the water, but not before the roots of the plants have had a chance to use up their share.

This product works fine, but please keep your expectations reasonable.Peat is used to soften the water and lower ph.  It does so by reducing carbonate hardness.  This is the water's buffering capacity.  Once the carbonate hardness has been lowered, the ph will start to drop.  The buffering capacity is the water's resistance to ph drops.  To drop the ph, you first have to lower the resistance.Peat may not work for you if your tap water is very hard.  A high GH usually accompanies a high KH (carbonate hardness).  If the water is too hard, peat alone may not be enough to lower your ph.  In my situation, the GH out of the tap is approximately 400-450ppm!  With water this hard, peat alone will not do the job.  You would first need to remove most of the hardness.  Which you can do, using several different methods.  Reverse Osmosis, Ion Exchange, or using rain water.

I use this to help with my angelfish, and as far as I've seen it does help a lot with the fungus, but sometimes you have to go a bit more on the dose to a really dark blue (it might fade to a lighter blue throughout a few days) to make sure that it's working correctly.

BitTwiddler has already done a good job of listing its many uses.  Other reviewers have done a pretty good job of suggesting alternative and creative uses for the product.  Not having had the motivation to try turning my urine blue, I shall confine my review to the product's use in the aquatic hobby.This is a product that is becoming hard to find at the local pet store.  Partly because there are products out there that can solve the same problems without the drawbacks of methylene blue.  As others have said, this product can stain the aquarium silicone and the tank ornaments.  From my experience, the stain will eventually fade away from silicone, but it can take a few water changes.  There are cure for Ich out there that are just as effective that will not stain your silicone.  Seachem Paraguard is a good example.  However, Methylene Blue, while an oldie is still a goodie.  There are many uses for it in the hobby.As others have pointed out, it is used prophylactically to prevent fungus from attacking fish eggs.  This is particularly useful for those fish eggs that are being hatched in very soft, acidic water.  This product is also used by online fish stores as a water additive when they bag fish for shipment.  If you order an expensive specimen from an online fish retailer, your order will most likely be shipped to you in water that has methylene blue added.  This helps prevent mold from growing inside the bag while the fish is in transit as well as lowering the chances of the fish succumbing to ammonia toxicity.  It is still a gentle, effective cure for Ich.This is one of those staple medications that would be useful to have in your fish medication cabinet.  While there are more convenient antibiotics to remedy some of the fungal and bacterial infections out there, there are indications that pathogens may be developing resistance to some of them.  From what I have been able to research, there has been no indication of fungus resistance to methylene blue.  Sometimes, if you find that pathogens are resisting your treatment, you may have to switch weapons.

This is a small, cheap, simple little filter. I have it hooked up to a very quiet pump (the one it comes with in the package deal isn't very nice) and plan on modifying it. Why modify it? Well, in order to cycle a tank (get beneficial, waste-eating bacteria to help get rid of ammonia, the #1 killer of fish) you have to keep the filter running for about a month without changing the cartridge. The waste-eating bacteria will be established in about a month, but as soon as you change the cartridge, the cycle starts over leaving you with deadly ammonia levels all over again. of course, this is just layman's terms, read up on cycling aquariums, it's virtually a necessity to keeping fish alive and also enables you to go substantially longer between water changes since toxins don't build up as quickly.Anyway, the problem with this filter is if you change your cartridge once a month or more your tank is never cycled, and even if you space them out less often you are putting your fish in month-long danger every time you change the cartridge. However, I believe there is a solution. I am cutting the plastic off top of the cartridge so I can change out the carbon with bulk carbon in a filter media bag and put it in so I can change out the carbon and leave the sponge. Alternately, I may buy cut-to-fit sponge so I have two sponges in the filter and just alternate which sponge I change every couple of weeks (that way there is always an older sponge in the filter, with the bacteria on it, and that sponge provides bacteria to the new sponge for a few weeks before the old sponge is changed).

A note to fish owners--you really shouldn't throw these out every few weeks like the packaging recommends, unless you're specifically using the carbon to get medication out of the water. Completely replacing these filters can actually be BAD for your aquarium because beneficial, toxin-removing organisms grow on the filters and naturally break down toxic fish waste into less harmful byproducts. If you get rid of these beneficial organisms by removing the filter media they inhabit, you can destroy the ability of your aquarium to naturally break down the deadly ammonia in your fish's waste. The carbon in the replacement filters is no substitute for a healthy bioload, and your aquarium's water chemistry can become unstable and dangerous to your fish, even with regular water changes. (Look up 'aquarium nitrogen cycle' for more info, or just look at all the reviews that talk about how their fish got sick or died after they replaced all their filters at once.)Instead, make a slit in the filter media, remove the carbon, and then rinse off the built-up gunk with NON-CHLORINATED water every few weeks (you can use the water you siphon out of your fish tank during water changes). You can use these filters until the actual filter media starts to wear thin and break down. Not only will you have a healthier aquarium, but you'll spend less on replacement filters!

I have 4 UV sterilizers in the 125 gallon tank and 1 UV Sterilizer in the 60 gallon tank. 800 dollars worth of UV sterilizers that I was lead to believe can keep ick out of a tank. Earlier this year, my 125 gallon tank with 4 UV sterilizers was wiped out of over 30 fish in the course of 3 to 5 days. This month, ick struck my 60 gallon tank without warning. Stress seems to be the number one factor of causing an outbreak of ick. I had two bully fish in the 125 gallon tank that were difficult to remove. One was actually deemed INSANE from my dealer who maintains the tanks. Then I had purchased conflicting fish that attacked each other for two days. At first they got along, then they started chasing each other all into the night. By the time I woke up, they were still battling for control. Every tank will have a  Boss . These factors created a perfect storm for ick to kill 30 of 35 fish. Ick is very deceptive. You may not notice it until it is too late. By the time your first fish dies, or shows signs of weakness, your tank is history. The live rock, corals, etc. all need to be treated. Fortunately I purchased the finest  live rock  that was available. After the treatments of the tank were completed, my dealer took each of the roughly 25 live rocks and cleaned them by hand. He also carefully scraped sediment off of the back of my tank with a small razor blade, giving the tank a brand new look. It took over 3 hours to do. Having one dealer, he kept a list of what I had in the tank and we were able to cross the bullies off of the list and rebuild the tank again.My backup tank now has an infection of ick. This time it was caused by stress, low salt levels and a group of fish that went crazy and started attacking other fish. They were large Salt Water Mono's (Silver Dollar Hooks) that flew over the cuckoo's nest and began attacking other fish.I was under the impression that UV Sterilizer's will keep ick away and protect the tanks. I learned the hard way that they do not do anything for an outbreak that occurs internally. An Ammonia test kit is an essential tool to have in your kit.  This inexpensive test kit will pay for itself many times over.A test kit is essential to have when you are trying to diagnose a problem in your tank.  There are many situations that can disrupt your biological filtration.  When one of those  events  happen to you, you will need to know the extent of the damage.  You can measure the extent of that damage by measuring the levels of ammonia in the water.So, what kind of an event can cause an ammonia spike in a mature fish tank?  Here's a scenario.  One of your fish dies.  And because it is a big tank with lots of decorations, you do not notice this until some time has passed.  A dead fish, decaying and rotting inside the tank, can really cause a big ammonia spike.  Uneaten food is almost as bad.  When your fish starts showing stress, like gasping at the surface, one of the things you need to do is test your water.  If your fish stops eating, you might want to start observing and look for obvious problems.  Look for signs of bullying and parasites.  And then test your water for ammonia, nitrite, and PH.This handy kit from API will serve you well and help you keep your fish healthy.  I know, testing is not high on the list of fun things to do.  The good news here is that you do not have to constantly test your water.  The only time that you will need to do constant testing is at the early stage when you first set up the tank.  You would want to monitor the levels of ammonia during this cycle process.  After that, as long as the water parameters have stabilized, you only will need to test whenever an event disrupts or damages the biological filtration.  Some fish medications can temporarily disrupt the bio filter.  Overfeeding can overwhelm the ability of the beneficial bacteria to cope with the increased ammonia load.  Power failure can cut the circulation to your filter media and temporarily depress its ability to decompose ammonia.  It's usually helpful to know the amount of ammonia in the system before you decide on how much water to change.  Changing 50% of the water will cut the ammonia present in the system by half.  However, if your tap water does not match the ph and the gh of your tank water, then such a massive water change will cause those two measures to fluctuate.  Some sensitive fish species will not like such a massive ph swing within a short amount of time.  Therefore, in such a scenario, you would only want to change out the amount of water necessary to bring ammonia down to safe levels.This kit is easy to use.  Basically, you will be adding reagents from two separate bottles.  Lots of shaking.  Wait 5 minutes.  And then compare the results with a color chart.The only thing that I would change about this test kit is the included glass vial.  It is made of thin glass.  This glass tube is fragile.  Fortunately, you can purchase replacement glass tubes from API.

Even when you think there's no more redness in the overflow, there will be some left.Empty as much water from the pot as you can, and scoop the substrate into a cup or a glass (I used a 2-cup measurer). If the aquarium is full of water, lower the cup bottom-first to the bottom of the tank, and spill the substrate around gently. Repeat, until it's all used up. The water will cloud  -  but will filter-clear in a day or two.I put 55 ounces in an aquarium about two months ago. It took a day-and-a-half for the cloudiness to clear.  Two days later I laid-in several live plants  -  Java Fern, Amazon Sword, and Anubius Nana. They are all thriving, growing, and looking great. I even like the rich brown color  -  the fish and plants look great with it. I just ordered two more 55-ounce packs.As far as the review claiming it lowered pH and killed ten fish, I can only wonder how that could happen, since  --1.) There is no known substance within a substrate that could possibly  lower pH that drastically (and that quickly!!) in a 40 gallon tank.2.) There is NOTHING in Laterite that could cause that to occur.3.) In fact, I put this product in a tank in which I was having a great deal of trouble lowering the pH, and it made no difference whatsoever.There MUST have been another cause.This is an excellent product. I have a 40 gallon modified breeder tank used to house a 4  mud turtle and a small number of gold and other fish.  The turtle needs 8-10hrs of light with decent heat to keep a normal circadian rhythm and appetite.  It is sensitive to water and air temperature changes.Turtle and fish appreciate plants, and I needed someway to fight algae.  We do have a plek but that isn't enough to handle that much light.  So, I have been slowly adding additional laterite substrate and plants until the plants can basically starve the algae out of food/energy.I've worked with river stones, crushed coral, and regular aquarium pebbles in the past.  Coral looks the best, but can be annoying when it gets sucked into the filter intake and the small pebbles can be ingested and get stuck in turtle stomachs.  River stones are excellent for decoration but just don't have pizazz and are no good for plants.  I don't want regular soil in the aquarium. Regular aquarium pebbles are no good for the plants.  Laterite has a nice decorative look, has perfect size, and is very good for the plants...so far, I'm happy with it.Except that there are two modest issues with putting the laterite in.* No matter how much you rinse it, you can't avoid it making the water cloudy for at least a few days.  My tank seems to take ~5 days of full speed filter running and a 50% water change to return to normal.* I do believe that in small tanks the laterite does have at least a moderate effect on ph, reducing it for at least the first week from 6.9 or so to 6.5 in my tank.  Water changes and calcium blocks or other higher ph substrate like coral can be used to keep everything in balance.  Also, I suspect that over time, the effect will be minimal.

Garlic has its many uses.  Aside from seasoning food, it has been used to kill fungus and bacteria since ancient times.  In the dark ages, it was used to ward off vampires.  Recently, claims have been made that it also helps lower your bad cholesterol as well as boosting your immune system.  The one very negative side effect is the odor it produces.  Garlic is something you want to avoid eating right before your social engagements.  If the smell is strong enough to drive away a horny Count Dracula, it most certainly will make you less attractive to your spouse.Don't worry.  All of the above concerns are of no importance in aquaculture.  Unlike your spouse, fish are actually attracted to the smell of garlic.  I know, it is hard to believe.  But this stuff works like a charm.  You can take a cube of frozen bloodworms and let it thaw out in a small container.  Add Garlic Guard to the food before feeding.  Watch your fish go wild.  As soon as the food hits the water, the fish will start going hyper.  This makes the food more attractive to the fish.I'm not saying Garlic Guard will have the same effect on your fish as fresh blood would to a school of piranhas.  But, you should be able to see a difference in how your fish will react to the food.  Perhaps you bought a new fish that refuses to eat.  Try soaking the food in Garlic Guard and see how it reacts.  You will be surprised.I am not going to discuss the other claims made for garlic products in general.  That it helps rid the fish of internal parasites.  Fortunately for me, I have not had to put this to the test.  Besides, I have other remedies at my disposal should internal parasites were to infect my fish again.  My preferred treatment for those are either Metronidazole, Fenbendazole, or Epsom Salt.  Depending on the parasite.  To me, the main value of this product is that it helps to make the food more attractive to the fish.  If you have ever used the New Life Spectrum brand of fish food, you know that one of its main ingredients is garlic.  If you are already feeding New Life Spectrum, adding Garlic Guard is not necessary.Be careful with this product.  If you spill it on your carpet, it will be difficult to remove the smell.  If the amount that spilled is small, you can try using Oxy-Clean.  But that is not guaranteed to work if the garlic has soaked down into the padding.  Handle with care.

I never thought I'd have to worry about a fish not wanting to eat, and even keeping discus, I've never had a problem... until I got  Meep  as my wife lovingly calls him.  Meep was a healthy looking little Royal Blue Discus when we bought him and he stayed quite happy in our tank for all of two weeks and made all sorts of friends with the other discus until I, in my clumsy human ways, moved a piece of driftwood that he liked to hide behind (thus the name).  Worst. Thing. Ever.  Meep's little world ended when that piece of wood moved all of six inches towards the back of the tank.  He stopped schooling with the other fish and visiting us at the front of the tank, he hid constantly, and most importantly, he stopped eating.  I let his temper tantrum go on for two or three days with little notice until I saw how skinny the little guy was becoming, and so our journey began.All the other fish were fat and happy, but Meep was scales and bones, and I was sure he was going to kill over any day from this hunger strike.  Flake food, pellets, frozen food (which he would usually devour), live food, the little guy wouldn't touch anything!  Thinking he was sick, I treated him for worms and intestinal parasites- no good!  Water changes, medication, expensive foods, had fed with a pair of tongs, he just didn't care!  The little guy still wouldn't eat.And so came in Garlic Guard as a sort of last resort.  I mean, I love garlic, but my fish?  I was dubious.  I threw in some blood worms without this product and, just as I suspected, Meep ignored them while all his one time friends happily devoured everything in sight.  Pouring a bit of Garlic Guard into a cup and adding some more bloodworms and letting them soak made ~me~ hungry from the smell alone- and did the trick for my stubborn fish too.  As soon as the worms hit the water Meep darted out from his hiding place and hesitantly approached one of the little red wigglers, and as if lulled by the intoxicating smell of garlic-flavored worms, he ate it.  And then ate some more.  Jump ahead a week into the future, my once near-dead hunger-strike fish has decided that life is worth living after all so long as garlic is involved.  He and I both give this product five stars.___Theatrics aside, this is a good product for getting picky eaters or sick fish more interested in their food.  I love Seachem stuff and am glad I have a bottle of this on hand now should I need to medicate any fish, and it has the added bonus of containing vitamin C.  It only takes a little bit each feeding so a large bottle will last a while.

Fish love bloodworms.  Even finicky eaters will eagerly accept bloodworms.  The most appealing form of bloodworms is naturally, live bloodworms.  Unfortunately, most hobbyists do not have the time to manage and farm bloodworms.  So, your choices are generally frozen or freeze dried.  The fish prefer frozen, but they will eagerly accept freeze-dried almost as enthusiastically.  And of the freeze-dried commercial foods in the market, Hikari seems to have the best reputation from hobbyists, as determined from internet forums.These are actually not worms, but rather insect larva.  They are not your typical strongyloid, internal parasite that you may find in livestock.  These  bloodworms  are similar to mosquito larva.  They sell them in different sizes.  Some are small, like mosquito larvae.  The ones that you can buy frozen from San Francisco Bay Brands are typically much larger, more than a half-inch long.  If you have smaller fish, say neon tetras, get the smaller variety.  You can even get frozen  glass worms , which are mosquito larva.  The Hikari freeze-dried product is the same size as mosquito larva.  Maybe they started out larger and the drying process cause them to shrink. I purchased some Hikari freeze dried brine shrimp to add a little variety in my fish's diet.They will hungrily gobble up freeze-dried blood worms, but these brine shrimp, they don't seem so keen on. One of my guppies got to it first, and ate plenty. It was one of the days when the fish would actually eat it.I noticed a little while later the guppy was bloated up. The freeze-dried food had expanded in his stomach. I watched him for signs of constipation. Later on the next day, I fed him a tiny bit of freeze-dried brine shrimp again, soaked this time (ironically, it's recommended for constipation as it works as a laxative in fish.) After that I starved him for a couple of days, he only got a tiny bit of flake food from the other fish.He pooped the largest poop I have ever seen a livebearer do. I figured he was OK then, he wasn't constipated.He had clamped his tailfin at this point. He had no other signs of disease. He didn't have bloat, he didn't have swim-bladder disease, he didn't have any infections. I kept watching him to make sure he was OK. He was eating normally. He was having difficulty swimming with his clamped tailfin. He slowly got weaker, then I noticed one night he was at the bottom of the tank, with his tailfin resting on the bottom, as if he couldn't swim. The next morning I noticed he had passed away.The bloating from the freeze-dried food must have damaged him internally, and he couldn't heal from it.Learn from my mistake, soak your freeze-dried food for at least several minutes before feeding it to your fish. Use tank water, not tap water.

During the summer of 2013 Doctors Foster & Smith was having its summer sale, so I decided to purchase a few Marineland filters:  Some HOT 250s and a 350 Magnum.The HOT 250 has become my maintenance filter of choice, doing many of the heavy clean up jobs that I used to use my *Vortex D-1 diatom filter for.  I purchased a new Vortex XL after my 30 + years old D-1 wore out, however, I just use this filter for the occasional diatoming of my aquariums, since it's still the best diatom filter on the market (IMHO).* You can even use diatom powder with the HOT 250 and 350 Magnum, however, it does not coat on the filter cartridges for these filters as well as it does onthe Vortex diatom filters.I use a Magnum 350 as the main canister filter on a Mr. Aqua 17.1 gallon rimless tank.  It's a bit of overkill given the 350's maximum 100 gallon rating. Nevertheless, the 350 works well on this tank, since its intake and output tubes have adjustable valves to control water flow.Because of the size of the 350, I only clean it twice a year.As for construction, it's not built like my Eheim or Fluval canister filters, however, it's built well enough and given its age, still a clever design.I also like the fact that it can be used as a micron filter.For those who have claimed that the 350 is not useful for biological filtration, I have found exactly the opposite.I would imagine that they are making this claim because they use charcoal in the center compartment of this filter instead of ceramic biological nodes.The fact is that the charcoal is largely unnecessary unless you are intent on removing  medications that you have used for treating your fishes, or water that has been stained from tanning.In fact, using charcoal for chemical filtration leaches carbon from your aquarium's water column which can deprive your plants of the necessary carbon uptake.As such, I load the center of my  Magnum 350 with biological filtration.  Along with the mechanical media the 350 works very well as a two stage canister filter.I also like the micron filter feature for both the 350 Magnum and the HOT 250, which gives these filters quite a bit of flexibility in keeping your aquarium's water nice and healthy.As for price, I don't believe that I have ever seen a canister filter with a greater price disparity on the Internet than I have with the Marineland 350 Magnum.I have seen this filter selling for over $300 on some Internet pet retail sites (without the biowheel attachment), and as little as $79.99 including shipping at Doctors Foster & Smith during their 2013 summer sale.At the $79.99 price the 350 is a bargain.  In my opinion  it is still a good value at $100. However, at more than $110 or so, there are better canister filters to be had.A couple of long-term 350 Magnum and HOT 250 users have stated that there's a readily available supply of parts for these filters, offered by Internet pet retailers.  While this is true, these parts can be expensive.In this fish-keeper's experience, it is better to wait until these filters (or virtually any aquarium component) are on sale, and then purchase two of them - one for spare parts. Then you've really got yourself a bargain.Highly recommended!

I wish the Filstar had a ceramic shaft and a better housing design to dampen vibration. That is why it is cheaper. Uses a steel shaft and doesn't have any rubber or softer plastic around the impeller housing to dampen sound. I hear some people get quiet ones and others do not. Mine isn't really loud, it just has a different humming frequency than my Fluval and I am not used to it and it is a little bit louder overall. So I placed a folded up towel on top of the filter and it absorbs the sound quite well. Now it is near silent. I also have it outside my stand which will make any canister noticeably more loud. My Fluval is within my other stand. I really want to figure out a way to make it quieter. I haven't come up with any good solutions, yet. I will keep plugging away until I do. I would highly recommend this filter.

There are many fish meds out there for external parasites.  The decision on which chemical to use will partly be dictated by the other inhabitants of your tank, as well as the external parasite that you are trying to remove.  Copper is very good for external parasites and will kill even the larger worms and leeches.  However, copper is not for the novice.  You should have a copper test kit if you want to use copper.  Paraguard is not as strong as copper and will probably not cure your fish of anchor worms and leeches.  What it does have going for it is that it is easy on the fish and, in my experience, it is safe for the plants.  This is a gentle medication for something like Ich and Velvet.Remove the carbon from your filter when using this product.  You may also get better results in treating Ich if you raise the temperature to 80-85 degrees Fahrenheit if your fish can tolerate it.  Feed sparingly when medicating, to keep from having to change out the water.  This will make it easier on you.  For Ich, this is not as fast as Quick Cure, but it seems gentler and does not hurt the plants.  It is your decision whether to raise the temperature or not.  If you choose not to, you may need to prolong the treatment just to make sure that you kill off every bit of the parasites.This medication is gentle enough that you can use it on your quarantine tank.  For example, you can assume that the fish that you bought have some latent infection and are carrying ectoparasites.  While in quarantine, you can medicate them with this and not cause undue stress.  My protocol is to first treat the new fish with medicated food blended with Fenbedazole and Seachem Focus.  That gets rid of internal worms.  Another week after and I add API's General Cure to the water.  If the fish species is sensitive, for example Ram cichlids, I may use Seachem Paraguard instead of General Cure.  Paraguard will not really help if the fish have Hexamita or Tapeworms.  But, I assume that the Fenbendazole took care of the tapeworms.Paraguard is good to have in your fish medicine cabinet.  For something like Ich and Velvet, it will be all that you need.  I would recommend that you have several types of medication in your cabinet.  These are the ones that I keep on hand: Seachem Paraguard, API General Cure, Fenbendazole, Focus, Methylene Blue, Cupramine, and Kanamycin.  All my tanks are freshwater.  I have only used Cupramine once.  Copper is not something that I would recommend as a first choice, unless you are prepared to test the water for copper concentration.  Too much can kill the fish very easily.  Stick with Paraguard for most external parasites like Ich.  Save the big guns for something hard to kill, like anchor worms, leeches, and flukes.

I'll add my version of what advice helped me mixed with my own experience for any new perspective buyers:1- WHAT YOU NEED: You should get a dual port pump, smaller pumps aren't strong enough. I tried a smaller single port for a few days as my air pump didn't arrive when my skimmer did, and it wasn't very efficient. Once my dual port whisper arrived boom!!! Great skimming for months now on same stone even... So get a good strong pump is MOST important for success. Also a small plastic air tube control valve is helpful in each line to start the air correctly, (unless your air pump has individual controls for each port) but not a necessity if you just unhook the line from the pump that you put air into second. Then after upflow is going hook it up. But then I used a valve on upflow too to turn it down some, so one on each side is helpful and they are cheap in the multi pack. You will need tubing of course.2- INSTRUCTIONS: there was a taped note on the upflow tube telling you your're supposed to start air to that tube first, as two air tubes come out of the top of it. (Idiot proof I would say). Do this and the flow works fine. Also tells you where the water line should be on the box if I recall. Again for that one poor soul that had it literally on the back of his tank, outside... Options are on back of your tank INSIDE your aquarium, or other choice probably best if possible is placement in a sump if you use one.3- QUALITY- it's made out of flimzy plastic yes, handle with care during installation. After instelation tho, removing and replacing the cup has been uneventful and easy. The removable cup for leaning stands well above waterline and above my flat hood so it had easy access. There are some bubbles that escapes the big column tube prior to the cup where the air tube comes out, but those few bubbles doesn't affect it's function. Initially I found it curious. It is a minor design distraction so don't stress if you see that, it hasn't affected the skimming at all.4- CONDITION: Mine arrived in fine working condition. But, if it comes broke, just send back for replacement. Once you get the right one (for those few cases that recieved broken parts) you will not regret replacing with an operational one. This thing skims with a lot do might daily!These were details for the newer tank hobbiest that are confused about the set up... I hope it helps solve any more confusions.

I thought this litter was a joke.  Some weird looking, politically correct,  green  gimmick litter.  Well, my cat got declawed (yes, I'm a terrible person but my children need their eyes), and the vet wanted me to use this litter because it is dustless.  I was SUPER hesitant.  Well, I was wrong.  It actually works remarkably well.  The best thing about this litter compared to the cheap, high rated litter I was using off Amazon and the Arm and Hammer Clump and Seal I later switched to is this litter has absolutely no odor, whether clean or dirty.  Even clean the Arm and Hammer has a chemical smell.  It is very good as covering urine smell (100% effective with my cat).  Poop smells really depend on how well the cat buried it as it would with any litter.  It is dustless, sort of.  After about a week there are a lot of small particles in the bottom of the litter pan, and those can make their way out of the box but that said there is less stray stuff than with the other two types of litter.  And even though the litter looks weird (almost like some little cylindrical animal poop) and I thought the cat might not like it, it used the litter without complaint.  So I used up the bag in two weeks like the vet asked, and I'm back to the Clump and Seal I already had.  The real question is what type of litter am I going to buy next.  I'm not sure.  Probably depends on the price but either this or the Clump and Seal.  Please keep in mind that I scoop litter twice a day when I feed the cat so I can't comment on how litter performs when scooped less often.  Another comment I want to add is that I've notice my cat (which is a Devon Rex and has unique fur, almost like a rabbit), sometimes smells like the clean arm and hammer litter and is  dusty  after she's been digging around when I'm hugging around on her and the dust even gets in my nose a bit which is, of course, unpleasant and makes me less fond of giving the cat attention.  This stuff does not do that.  Also, after reading I see some people had trouble using the litter.  I did not use much at all in the pan, certainly not over an inch.  I have excellent lighting (large office like fluorescent lights) so I could easily distinguish poop.  Litter that had been urinated on became more black and swollen and I would pick that up with a high quality scoop and just throw it out without any sifting (you don't sift at all with this litter) and poop I just picked up and tossed.  After about a week the litter was barely covering the bottom of the pan and there were a lot of little particles and I pitched it all.  I did not use a liner or ever have trouble with  congealed  litter, but, again, I scoop twice daily and used a small amount and have good lighting so maybe this is why I had different, better results than some.

This filter sponge works with the Aquaclear brand of aquarium power filters.  This one is specifically sized for the model 20/mini.  Unlike your typical power filter media, this one can simply be rinsed and re-used instead of replaced.  This money-saving design is perhaps the best feature of the Aquaclear system.This foam block is made out of a material that will not wear out in a typical aquarium environment.  However, if you have a tank that produces a lot of debris, say if you keep plants like Java Moss, it is possible to get the foam clogged to the point that it will take a lot of work to get all of the debris out.  At that point, rather than spending all of that effort, you may just be better off replacing the sponge.Why 4 stars instead of 5?  In my opinion, the coarse design of the sponge media allows too much smaller particles to get through.  By that, I mean that it is not as good as clearing cloudy water as a floss-type filter media.  The Aquaclear design also seems to allow more water by-pass than most of its competitors.  This is a review of the filter sponge media, however, it is hard to review this without taking the design of the whole filtration system into consideration.Now, what can you do with your clogged filter sponge after you've decided to replace it with a new sponge?  You can rinse out and use it as a substrate for your plants.  For example, if you go to your local pet shop and view the plants, you will find a lot of them now come in small, sealed, plastic bags.  These plants were grown using tissue culturing, and they come to you rooted in a gel medium.  This method has a lot of advantages (no snails, algae, or parasites hitchhiking on the plant!) to you.  All you would need to do is remove some of the gel from the roots and your plant is ready for your tank.  However, you can increase the chances of the plant's survival if you use this foam instead of simply planting the roots in your gravel.  You can take a used (or new) Aquaclear filter sponge, cut a slit, and insert your new plant into the sponge, including the gel.  Not long after, you will see your new plant growing on the sponge.  Now, obviously, plants growing on a sponge do not make a pretty picture.  It does work and may be a worthwhile option for those people who have tried growing plants on their substrate and failed.  If you have deep enough gravel bed, you can bury and hide the sponge.  Having said all of this, I did not consider this alternative use in writing the review.  After all, the review should be about how well the product performs its intended function.  I just wanted to present this to give you an option to recycle your old sponge.

edit:4/8/14Love the canister so much, I got a second one for another tank (still waiting for tank to be delivered)!  Same as first canister: great quality product, comes with useful media, easy to put together, no leaks, and runs silent.  Have it hooked up to the same tank as the original right now to start cycling it to build up beneficial bacteria while waiting on the tank to arrive.Original review:I recently bought one of these and I have to say, I'll never use another brand of canister filter besides eheim again.The sunsun cansiter filter I have in the next room that's been running since last October is loud (hums/vibrates) and its flow/pressure isn't enough to keep mulm from building up and clogging the spray bar.. oh did I mention its filter floss crap pads it comes with suck and you have to buy all the media? I've had to clean out that canister a few times and its a real pain.  The sunsun I got comes with a uv sterilizing light but I can't for the life of me get at it to turn it off or replace it (imposible to remove plastic  cap  over it)  honestly I don't think its helped much though..  The plastic for its intake/output is flimsy and its suction cups too weak to handle the rigid hose (had to buy extra suction cups)  Again that's is the sunsun I'm bashing just now.By comparison the Ehiem came with all the media needed (good quality media too!) could barely cram in the  seed media  from existing tank filters to help speed up cycling.  I placed the eheim right under my desk.  Its so quiet I'd forget its there if not for the sound of water coming from the outflow (have water level a little low so more agitation=more aeration for cycling).  Love the shut off valves for the tubing to take it apart for maintenance etc.  Suction cups that come with this works great as do the very small but rigid piping for inlet/outlet (but not a huge fan of the green color).Learned a little trick: after you separate the canister filter and move it to a sink or somewhere safe to remove the lid, open up the intake hose again and unlatch the little metal hook, the lid comes off much easier.If you want a canister filter splurge and get the eheim!  You'll get good quality.  But people say the 2211/ 40 gallon  rated one doesn't really have enough umf for 40 gallons.  I have mine on a 7 gallon right now and am sure it would work up through a 20, but not sure about 40.  If you want an eheim for a larger tank, get the next size up.  I'll probably replace my other canister (the sunsun) with the largest eheim model I can get.Only thing I don't like is the same for EVERY canister: that ugly green semi translucent tubing, give me 100% clear or give me solid not both x.xAnyways bottom line: BUY IIIITTTT

I have this filter on a 20 gallon and it's perfect. It's been running for a year now with no problems. Comes with everything needed so it's ready to use right out the box. Just a heads up invest in a big roll of filter floss and cut it to fix. It will save you a lot of money in the long run. Especially if your like me and like to replace the floss every three weeks.

Easy to install,  see youtube videos for help with minor things.  Should have a 90 elbow for the tube, but got one from Homedepot.  The units is virtually silent.  Works well.  All the reviews about this filter are true.  One of the bench marks of canister filters.

Seriously, you cannot beat an eheim canister filter. Comes with media, ball valves so basically ready to go out of the box. Took me about 15min to set up. You also don't have to suck water through the hose to fill. As long as the filter is below the tank, hook everything up, with the ball valves closed. Insert the in and out puts. Open the ball valve on the input, water will start to flow, open the output ball valve and you will have a full filter in minutes. For once I didn't make a mess on the carpet starting a filter. Very Very Very pleased. After the initial set up, the canister will be a bit noisey from air bubbles. Tilt the filter around, give it a bit of a shake and let it run wide open throttle for about 30 min, then adjust it to where you want. Mine runs silent now!I have this set up on an 8.7 bowfront tank, over filtration for sure, but you can't go wrong with that.

In five years, I have had three canister filters fail.  (Check my other reviews)  I decided to give a classic brand and a trusted design a try.  My last filter (Penn Plax Cascade) started leaking, and for two weeks my tank had no filtration (the Fluval replacement for the Cascade broke upon installation).  When the Eheim arrived, I thought I must have made a mistake and ordered one for a smaller tank.  It was half the size of other canister filters.  But, no, it was for a 40 gallon tank.  In 48 hours my tank is crystal clear.  The canister is totally silent (I have to touch it to feel if it is working).  I'm surprised it does such a good job with such gentle water circulation (the Cascade would hurl fish into cartwheels if they got near the water output nozzle).I would give this five stars except that the installation instructions were not only incomprehensible, but wrong.  There was filter medium sent with the canister that was not even pictured in the instructions.  I have no idea what the bag of little balls are.  I will probably change them out to carbon, because I don't think the carbon  pad  is adequate for removing toxins.I hope THIS filter lives as long a life as some have claimed in their reviews.  I shouldn't have to buy a new canister every 18 months.

You will see hundreds of reviews here swearing by these.  Most of them tout how they have been using eheim classics for years.
